### Do all the processes have the same proportion of defectives? {#sec-prc-46}

[**The contingency table approach**]{#sec-prc-46-contingency-table}

[**Testing for homogeneity of proportions using the chi-square distribution via contingency tables**]{#sec-prc-46-homogeneity-test}

When we have samples from $n$ populations (i.e., lots, vendors, production runs, etc.), we can test whether there are significant differences in the proportion defectives for these populations using a contingency table approach. The contingency table we construct has two rows and $n$ columns.

To test the null hypothesis of no difference in the proportions among the $n$ populations

$$ \mbox{H}_0: \,\,\, p_1 = p_2 = \cdots = p_n $$

against the alternative that not all $n$ population proportions are equal

$$ \mbox{H}_a: \,\,\, \mbox{Not all } p_i \mbox{ are equal } (i = 1, \, 2, \, \ldots, \, n) \, , $$

[**The chi-square test statistic**]{#sec-prc-46-test-statistic}

we use the following test statistic:

$$ \chi^2 = \sum_{\mbox{all cells}} \frac{(f_o - f_c)^2}{f_c} \, , $$

where $f_o$ is the observed frequency in a given cell of a $2 \times n$ contingency table, and $f_c$ is the theoretical count or expected frequency in a given cell if the null hypothesis were true.

[**The critical value**]{#sec-prc-46-critical-value}

The critical value is obtained from the $\chi^2$ distribution table with degrees of freedom $(2-1)(n-1) = n-1$, at a given level of significance.

**An illustrative example**

[**Data for the example**]{#sec-prc-46-data}

Diodes used on a printed circuit board are produced in lots of size 4000. To study the homogeneity of lots with respect to a demanding specification, we take random samples of size 300 from 5 consecutive lots and test the diodes. The results are:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-prc-46-observed
#| tbl-cap: "Observed frequencies by lot"
#| code-fold: true
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(gt)

nonconforming <- c(36, 46, 42, 63, 38)
conforming <- c(264, 254, 258, 237, 262)
lot_totals <- nonconforming + conforming

observed <- tibble(
  Results = c("Nonconforming", "Conforming", "Totals"),
  `1` = c(nonconforming[1], conforming[1], lot_totals[1]),
  `2` = c(nonconforming[2], conforming[2], lot_totals[2]),
  `3` = c(nonconforming[3], conforming[3], lot_totals[3]),
  `4` = c(nonconforming[4], conforming[4], lot_totals[4]),
  `5` = c(nonconforming[5], conforming[5], lot_totals[5]),
  Totals = c(sum(nonconforming), sum(conforming), sum(lot_totals))
)

observed |>
  gt() |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Lot", columns = c(`1`, `2`, `3`, `4`, `5`)) |>
  tab_style(
    style = list(cell_borders(sides = "top", weight = px(2)), cell_text(weight = "bold")),
    locations = cells_body(rows = Results == "Totals")
  )
```

[**Computation of the overall proportion of nonconforming units**]{#sec-prc-46-pbar}

Assuming the null hypothesis is true, we can estimate the single overall proportion of nonconforming diodes by pooling the results of all the samples as

$$ \bar{p} = \frac{36 + 46 + 42 + 63 + 38}{5(300)} = \frac{225}{1500} = 0.15 \, . $$

```{r}
#| label: verify-prc-46-pbar
#| code-fold: true
pbar <- sum(nonconforming) / sum(lot_totals)

tibble(Statistic = "$\\bar{p}$", Value = pbar) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, align = "lr")
```

[**Computation of the overall proportion of conforming units**]{#sec-prc-46-expected}

We estimate the proportion of conforming ("good") diodes by the complement 1 - 0.15 = 0.85. Multiplying these two proportions by the sample sizes used for each lot results in the expected frequencies of nonconforming and conforming diodes. These are presented below:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-prc-46-expected
#| tbl-cap: "Expected frequencies by lot"
#| code-fold: true
expected_nonconforming <- pbar * lot_totals
expected_conforming <- (1 - pbar) * lot_totals

expected <- tibble(
  Results = c("Nonconforming", "Conforming", "Totals"),
  `1` = c(expected_nonconforming[1], expected_conforming[1], lot_totals[1]),
  `2` = c(expected_nonconforming[2], expected_conforming[2], lot_totals[2]),
  `3` = c(expected_nonconforming[3], expected_conforming[3], lot_totals[3]),
  `4` = c(expected_nonconforming[4], expected_conforming[4], lot_totals[4]),
  `5` = c(expected_nonconforming[5], expected_conforming[5], lot_totals[5]),
  Totals = c(sum(expected_nonconforming), sum(expected_conforming), sum(lot_totals))
)

expected |>
  gt() |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Lot", columns = c(`1`, `2`, `3`, `4`, `5`)) |>
  tab_style(
    style = list(cell_borders(sides = "top", weight = px(2)), cell_text(weight = "bold")),
    locations = cells_body(rows = Results == "Totals")
  )
```

[**Null and alternate hypotheses**]{#sec-prc-46-hypotheses}

To test the null hypothesis of homogeneity or equality of proportions

$$ \mbox{H}_0: \,\,\, p_1 = p_2 = \cdots = p_5 $$

against the alternative that not all 5 population proportions are equal

$$ \mbox{H}_a: \,\,\, \mbox{Not all } p_i \mbox{ are equal } (i = 1, \, 2, \, \ldots, \, 5) \, , $$

[**Table for computing the test statistic**]{#sec-prc-46-calculations}

we use the observed and expected values from the tables above to compute the $\chi^2$ test statistic. The calculations are presented below:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-prc-46-chisq-calc
#| tbl-cap: "Chi-square calculations"
#| code-fold: true
fo <- c(nonconforming, conforming)
fc <- c(expected_nonconforming, expected_conforming)

chisq_calc <- tibble(
  fo_col = c(fo, NA),
  fc_col = c(fc, NA),
  diff_col = c(fo - fc, NA),
  diff2_col = c((fo - fc)^2, NA),
  contrib_col = c((fo - fc)^2 / fc, sum((fo - fc)^2 / fc))
)

chisq_calc |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    fo_col = html("f<sub>o</sub>"),
    fc_col = html("f<sub>c</sub>"),
    diff_col = html("(f<sub>o</sub> &minus; f<sub>c</sub>)"),
    diff2_col = html("(f<sub>o</sub> &minus; f<sub>c</sub>)<sup>2</sup>"),
    contrib_col = html("(f<sub>o</sub> &minus; f<sub>c</sub>)<sup>2</sup> / f<sub>c</sub>")
  ) |>
  sub_missing(columns = everything(), missing_text = "") |>
  fmt_number(columns = everything(), decimals = 3) |>
  tab_style(
    style = list(cell_borders(sides = "top", weight = px(2)), cell_text(weight = "bold")),
    locations = cells_body(rows = 11)
  ) |>
  cols_width(contrib_col ~ px(160), everything() ~ px(90)) |>
  tab_options(table.width = pct(100))
```

```{r}
#| label: verify-prc-46-chisq
#| code-fold: true
chi2_stat <- sum((fo - fc)^2 / fc)
chi2_crit <- qchisq(0.95, 4)
p_value <- 1 - pchisq(chi2_stat, 4)

tibble(Statistic = c("$\\chi^2$", "Critical value $\\chi^2_{0.95,4}$", "$p$-value"), Value = c(chi2_stat, chi2_crit, p_value)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 5, align = "lr")
```

[**Conclusions**]{#sec-prc-46-conclusions}

If we choose a 0.05 level of significance, the critical value of $\chi^2$ with 4 degrees of freedom is 9.488 (see the [chi square distribution table](#sec-eda-chi-square-distribution-table) in Chapter 1). Since the test statistic (12.131) exceeds this critical value, we reject the null hypothesis.
